questions.stem: Which situation is a pure risk?

choices.text: Buying a rental house to resell it
choices.rationale: Incorrect: an investment can produce a gain, so it is speculative.

choices.text: A tree could fall on your parked car
choices.rationale: Correct: the only outcomes are loss or no loss, so it is a pure risk.

choices.text: Betting on the outcome of a game
choices.rationale: Incorrect: gambling offers a chance of gain — speculative risk.
Incorrect: a business venture can profit or lose — speculative risk.

questions.explanation: Pure risk has only two outcomes — loss or no loss — and is the only kind insurers cover. Speculative risk adds the possibility of gain.

questions.stem: In personal auto insurance, an insured car is an example of a(n):

choices.rationale: Correct: an exposure is the unit of measure used to describe the risk an insurer takes on and to set premium.
Incorrect: a peril is a cause of loss, such as collision or theft.
Incorrect: a hazard is a condition that increases the chance or severity of loss.
Incorrect: a loss is the reduction in value after a peril strikes.

questions.explanation: Exposure measures how much risk is insured — for example, each car, dwelling or driver. More exposure units mean more chances of loss and more premium.

questions.scenario: Leo keeps a kerosene heater a few inches from the living room curtains in his rented apartment.
questions.stem: The heater's placement is best described as a:

choices.rationale: Incorrect: moral hazard involves dishonesty or intent to cause or exaggerate a loss.
Incorrect: morale hazard is indifference caused by having insurance; this is a physical condition.
Incorrect: fire would be the peril; the heater placement is a condition that makes fire more likely.
Correct: a tangible condition that increases the chance of a fire loss is a physical hazard.

questions.explanation: Hazards increase the chance or severity of loss. Physical hazards are tangible conditions — faulty wiring, icy steps, a heater beside curtains. The peril is the fire itself.
questions.memoryTip: If you can touch it, it's a physical hazard.

questions.scenario: Ana stops locking her car because "the insurance will pay if it's stolen." Her neighbor Rob plans to report his old car stolen after secretly selling it for parts.
questions.stem: Which hazards do Ana and Rob present?

choices.text: Ana: moral hazard; Rob: morale hazard
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this reverses the two; dishonesty is moral, carelessness is morale.
Incorrect: neither situation is a tangible condition of property.

choices.text: Ana: morale hazard; Rob: moral hazard
choices.rationale: Correct: Ana is careless because she has insurance (morale); Rob intends to deceive (moral).
Incorrect: Rob's planned deception is dishonesty, a moral hazard.

questions.explanation: A moral hazard comes from a person's dishonesty — such as planning a false theft claim. A morale hazard is carelessness or indifference to loss because insurance exists — such as leaving a car unlocked.

keyPoints.label: Ana is careless because of insurance (morale)

questions.stem: Each of the following is a peril EXCEPT:

choices.rationale: Incorrect: lightning is a cause of loss — a peril.
Incorrect: theft is a cause of loss — a peril.
Correct: a frayed cord is a physical hazard that makes a fire more likely; it is not itself a cause of loss.
Incorrect: windstorm is a cause of loss — a peril.

questions.explanation: A peril causes a loss (fire, lightning, theft, windstorm, collision). A hazard increases its likelihood or severity (a frayed cord). The resulting damage is the loss.

questions.scenario: Worried about the liability of owning a swimming pool, the Garcias decide not to install one at their new home.
questions.stem: Which method of handling risk are they using?

choices.rationale: Incorrect: reduction would be installing a fence or alarm to make the pool safer.
Correct: eliminating the activity eliminates the risk entirely.
Incorrect: transfer would be buying liability insurance for the pool.
Incorrect: retention would be keeping the pool and paying any losses themselves.

questions.explanation: Avoidance means not engaging in the activity that creates the risk. It is effective but often impractical for necessities such as driving or owning a home.
questions.memoryTip: Avoid = don't do it at all.

questions.scenario: To lower her premium, Bea raises the deductible on her homeowners policy from $500 to $2,500.
questions.stem: Raising the deductible is an example of:

choices.rationale: Correct: Bea keeps (retains) the first $2,500 of each covered loss.
Incorrect: a deductible does not lower the chance or size of a loss; it changes who pays.
Incorrect: she still owns the home and faces the same risks.
Incorrect: sharing spreads a risk among several parties who each bear part of it.

questions.explanation: Retention means accepting part or all of a risk and paying losses yourself. Deductibles and self-insurance are forms of retention. Reduction, by contrast, changes the loss itself — smoke detectors, sprinklers, alarms.

keyPoints.label: She pays the first part of each loss

questions.scenario: Three siblings jointly own a lake cabin and agree in writing that each will pay one-third of any uninsured damage.
questions.stem: This arrangement illustrates:

choices.rationale: Incorrect: they still own the cabin and face its risks.
Incorrect: no insurer takes on the uninsured damage.
Incorrect: the agreement does not lower the chance or size of loss.
Correct: the risk is spread among several people who each bear part of any loss.

questions.explanation: Sharing distributes a risk among a group so that each member bears a portion. Insurance itself is built on sharing, but here the siblings share the uninsured portion directly.
questions.memoryTip: Share = split the loss among the group.

questions.stem: Installing a central-station burglar alarm in a home is an example of which risk method?

choices.rationale: Incorrect: the homeowner still owns property that can be stolen.
Incorrect: retention is paying losses yourself.
Incorrect: transfer shifts the financial burden to someone else.
Correct: the alarm lowers the likelihood and severity of a theft loss.

questions.explanation: Risk reduction (loss control) lowers the chance or severity of loss: alarms, deadbolts, smoke detectors, sprinklers and anti-theft devices.
questions.memoryTip: Reduce = make the loss less likely or smaller.

questions.scenario: A homeowner hires a contractor whose agreement includes a hold-harmless clause making the contractor responsible for injuries caused by the contractor's work.
questions.stem: The hold-harmless clause is an example of:

choices.rationale: Incorrect: no insurance policy is involved in the clause itself.
Incorrect: the homeowner is shifting, not keeping, the risk.
Correct: the clause shifts the financial consequences of certain losses to the contractor by agreement.
Incorrect: the work still takes place.

questions.explanation: Risk can be transferred by purchasing insurance or by contract, such as a hold-harmless or indemnity agreement. Both shift the financial burden of a loss to another party.

questions.stem: For a homeowners insurer, each of the following is an element of an insurable risk EXCEPT:

choices.text: There are many similar exposure units in the group
choices.rationale: Incorrect: a large group of similar units is required to predict losses.

choices.text: The loss is intentionally caused by the insured
choices.rationale: Correct: an insurable loss must be accidental, not intentional.

choices.text: The loss is definite in time and measurable
choices.rationale: Incorrect: the cause, time, place and amount must be determinable.

choices.text: The premium is economically feasible for buyers
choices.rationale: Incorrect: the cost must be affordable relative to the potential loss.

questions.explanation: Insurable risks involve many similar exposure units, accidental losses, definite and measurable losses, no catastrophic concentration, a calculable chance of loss and an affordable premium.

questions.stem: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood mainly because flood:

choices.text: Can damage a large share of exposures in one event
choices.rationale: Correct: catastrophic potential across many insureds at once violates an element of insurable risk.

choices.text: Cannot be measured in dollars after it occurs
choices.rationale: Incorrect: flood damage is measurable.

choices.text: Is a speculative risk offering a chance of gain
choices.rationale: Incorrect: flood is a pure risk.

choices.text: Is always caused intentionally by the insured
choices.rationale: Incorrect: floods are generally accidental.

questions.explanation: An insurable risk should not expose the insurer to catastrophic loss affecting many units at once. Flood and earthquake can strike thousands of homes in one event, so they are excluded from standard homeowners forms and handled separately.

questions.scenario: As a hurricane approaches, many coastal homeowners who never carried windstorm coverage suddenly try to buy it.
questions.stem: This behavior illustrates:

choices.rationale: Correct: people with a higher-than-average chance of loss seek insurance more than others.
Incorrect: that principle concerns predicting losses across large groups.
Incorrect: buying coverage is transfer, and they still face the storm.
Incorrect: morale hazard is carelessness caused by having insurance.

questions.explanation: Adverse selection is the tendency of higher-risk people to buy or keep insurance. Insurers counter it with underwriting and with rules that limit binding coverage when a loss is imminent.
questions.memoryTip: Adverse selection = the riskiest line up first.

questions.stem: According to the law of large numbers, as the number of similar insured homes increases:

choices.text: The chance any one home burns decreases
choices.rationale: Incorrect: each home's individual risk is unchanged.
Incorrect: better predictability does not require higher premiums.

choices.text: The insurer can predict which home will burn
choices.rationale: Incorrect: insurers predict how many losses, not which ones.

choices.text: Actual losses come closer to predicted losses
choices.rationale: Correct: larger groups make loss predictions more accurate.

questions.explanation: The law of large numbers holds that the larger the group of similar exposure units, the more closely actual results match expected results. It lets insurers price coverage reliably.

questions.scenario: Coastline Mutual insures 30,000 homes near the shore. It pays another company to take on part of its potential hurricane losses.
questions.stem: In this arrangement, Coastline Mutual is the:

choices.rationale: Incorrect: the reinsurer is the company accepting the risk.
Incorrect: brokers place coverage; they do not cede their own risk.
Correct: the insurer that transfers part of its risk to a reinsurer is the ceding insurer.
Incorrect: purchasing groups are buyers of liability coverage, not primary insurers ceding risk.

questions.explanation: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. The ceding (primary) insurer transfers part of its risk to a reinsurer, protecting itself against catastrophic losses. Policyholders still deal with the primary insurer.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a risk retention group and a risk purchasing group?

choices.text: Retention groups cover property; purchasing groups cover only auto
choices.rationale: Incorrect: both are mainly liability arrangements for businesses with similar exposures.

choices.text: Retention group members own the insurer; a purchasing group buys from an insurer
choices.rationale: Correct: a risk retention group is a member-owned insurer, while a purchasing group buys coverage as a group from an existing insurer.

choices.text: Purchasing group members own the insurer; retention groups buy coverage
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this reverses the two.

choices.text: Retention groups are government programs; purchasing groups are private
choices.rationale: Incorrect: neither is a government insurance program.

questions.explanation: Both serve businesses with similar liability exposures. A risk retention group forms and owns its own insurer and retains the risk; a risk purchasing group pools its buying power to purchase liability insurance from an existing insurer.
questions.memoryTip: RETENTION retains (owns the insurer); PURCHASING purchases.

keyPoints.label: Purchasing group buys from an insurer

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts stock and mutual insurers?

choices.text: Policyholders own stock insurers; stockholders own mutuals
choices.rationale: Incorrect: this reverses the ownership.

choices.text: Stockholders own stock insurers; policyholders own mutuals
choices.rationale: Correct: ownership is the defining difference.

choices.text: The state owns mutuals; stockholders own stock insurers
choices.rationale: Incorrect: mutuals are private and owned by policyholders.

choices.text: Agents own stock insurers; policyholders own mutuals
choices.rationale: Incorrect: agents do not own stock insurers.

questions.explanation: A stock insurer is owned by stockholders, who may receive dividends from profits. A mutual insurer is owned by its policyholders and may return excess premium as nonguaranteed policy dividends.

questions.stem: Which feature best describes a fraternal benefit society?

choices.text: It is a nonprofit organization that insures its members
choices.rationale: Correct: fraternals are social, religious or service organizations providing insurance to members.

choices.text: It is owned by outside investors seeking profit
choices.rationale: Incorrect: that describes a stock insurer.

choices.text: It is a marketplace of individual underwriters
choices.rationale: Incorrect: that describes a Lloyd's association.

choices.text: It is a federal program for unavailable coverage
choices.rationale: Incorrect: that describes a government insurer such as the NFIP.

questions.explanation: Fraternal benefit societies are nonprofit organizations with a lodge or similar system that provide insurance — mainly life and health — to their members.

questions.stem: In a Lloyd's association, who actually assumes the insured risk?

choices.text: The Lloyd's association as a single company
choices.rationale: Incorrect: the association provides the marketplace, not the insurance.

choices.text: The policyholders, who own the association
choices.rationale: Incorrect: that describes a mutual insurer.

choices.text: A state guaranty fund backing the policy
choices.rationale: Incorrect: the association is not a guaranty fund.
Correct: individual members and syndicates each accept a share of the risk.

questions.explanation: A Lloyd's association is a marketplace. Individual underwriting members, often grouped into syndicates, assume the risks. Lloyd's of London is the best-known example and often writes unusual or high-value risks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a government insurance program used in personal lines?

choices.text: A syndicate within a Lloyd's association
choices.rationale: Incorrect: Lloyd's syndicates are private.
Incorrect: mutual insurers are private companies.
Correct: the NFIP is a federal flood insurance program.
Incorrect: stock insurers are private companies.

questions.explanation: Most personal lines coverage is written by private insurers. Government programs fill gaps where private coverage is unavailable or unaffordable — flood insurance through the federal NFIP is the classic personal lines example.

questions.scenario: An insurer incorporated in Ohio holds a certificate of authority to sell auto insurance in New York.
questions.stem: In New York, this insurer is a(n):

choices.rationale: Incorrect: alien insurers are formed outside the United States.
Incorrect: domestic insurers are formed in New York.
Correct: formed in another U.S. state = foreign; authorized in New York = admitted.
Incorrect: holding a certificate of authority makes it admitted.

questions.explanation: Domestic = formed in this state; foreign = another U.S. state; alien = another country. Admitted (authorized) insurers hold a certificate of authority in the state; nonadmitted insurers do not.
questions.memoryTip: Foreign = another STATE; alien = another COUNTRY.

questions.stem: A nonadmitted insurer is one that:

choices.text: Is incorporated outside the United States
choices.rationale: Incorrect: that is an alien insurer, which may be admitted or not.

choices.text: Has no certificate of authority in the state
choices.rationale: Correct: nonadmitted (unauthorized) insurers are not licensed to do business in the state.

choices.text: Has a low financial strength rating from A.M. Best
choices.rationale: Incorrect: ratings do not determine admission.
Incorrect: lines written have nothing to do with admission.

questions.explanation: Admission refers to authorization by the state. A nonadmitted insurer lacks a certificate of authority; its coverage can be accessed only in limited circumstances through specially licensed excess or surplus lines brokers.

questions.stem: An insurer incorporated in Bermuda that insures a home in New York is a(n):

choices.rationale: Correct: an insurer formed outside the United States is alien.
Incorrect: foreign insurers are formed in another U.S. state.
Incorrect: domestic insurers are formed in the state where they do business.
Incorrect: fraternal describes organization type, not place of incorporation.

questions.explanation: Classification by place of incorporation: domestic (this state), foreign (another U.S. state), alien (outside the U.S.).

questions.stem: What do independent rating services such as A.M. Best primarily evaluate?

choices.text: The fairness and accuracy of an insurer's advertising
choices.rationale: Incorrect: advertising is a regulatory matter, not the focus of financial ratings.

choices.text: Whether each of the insurer's agents is properly licensed
choices.rationale: Incorrect: licensing is handled by the state insurance department.

choices.text: The accuracy of each individual claim payment
choices.rationale: Incorrect: rating services assess the company's overall finances.

choices.text: An insurer's financial strength and ability to pay claims
choices.rationale: Correct: ratings reflect financial strength and claims-paying ability.

questions.explanation: Independent rating services (A.M. Best, Standard & Poor's, Moody's, Fitch) assign grades reflecting an insurer's financial strength. A rating is an opinion, not a guarantee.
questions.memoryTip: Ratings grade the wallet, not the ads.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the independent agency system from the exclusive agency system?

choices.text: The independent agent represents only one insurer
choices.rationale: Incorrect: independent agents represent several insurers.

choices.text: The exclusive agent is a salaried employee of a broker
choices.rationale: Incorrect: exclusive agents represent one insurer, not a broker.

choices.text: The exclusive agent owns the expirations
choices.rationale: Incorrect: under exclusive agency the insurer usually owns them.

choices.text: The independent agent usually owns the expirations
choices.rationale: Correct: under the independent agency system the agent owns the renewal records.

questions.explanation: Independent (American) agents represent multiple insurers and usually own the expirations, so they can move clients' business. Exclusive (captive) agents represent one insurer, which usually owns the expirations. Direct writers use employees; direct response uses mail, phone or internet.
